la:verb:coepi.html:
coepĭo, coepi, coeptum, 3 (the
tempp. press. only a few times in the ante-class. period, and coepturus, ; ; ; ; ; the tempp. perff., both in act. and pass. form, very freq.; a trisyl. coëpit, Lachm. N. cr.), v. a. and n.
contr. from co-ăpio = apo; hence coapias for coepias in Cod. Ambros.; ; v.in the foll., and cf. Lachm. ad
, lit. to lay hold of something on different sides, to lay hold of; hence of an action, to begin, commence, undertake ( = incipio, which is the class. pres.).
Act.
Tempp. press.: coepiam seditiosa verba loqui, Cato ap. Paul. ex Müll. lubido extemplo coepere est convivium, : mage si exigere coepias, Ritschl N. cr.: neque pugnas neque ego lites coepio,: ubi nihil habeat, alium quaestum coepiat,: mane coepiam, Caecil. ap. : non Prius olfecissem, quam ille quicquam coeperet, Fleck.; cf. Neue, Formenl. 2, 616: se Hasdrubalem adgressurum, ceterum non ante coepturum, quam, etc.,: nos rite coepturi ab Homero videmur,: nemine opinante quidnam coepturus esset,.—
Tempp. perff. act.; the object usu. an inf.; so always in Cic. and Cæs.; mostly an inf. act.; rarely pass.; sometimes the acc. of a noun or pronoun.
With inf. act.: cum ver esse coeperat,; : discere coepit, ap. Fest. s. v. sam, p. 325, 24 Müll. (v. 228 Vahl.): amare coepi,: oppugnare,: ire foras coeperunt,: coeperit inter se vesci, etc., et saep.—
With inf. pass. (in the poets and histt.): per terrarum orbem fruges coepisse creari,: alia hujuscemodi fieri coepere,: cum Lacedaemoniis pugnari coepit,; so, urbanus haberi,: verti,: institui,: moveri,; : expleri,: eligi,: occidi,: prohiberi,: coeptum est fieri, Auct. B. Afr. 69; 78; ; ; .—
With acc. (rare in prose; cf. B. infra): coepit cursum, Att. ap. : novam mapalibus urbem,: cur non ego id perpetrem, quod coepi?: si quicquam hodie hic turbae coeperis,: quae coeperamus,: hujuscemodi orationem,. 37: (Sabinus) obsidium coepit per praesidia,.—
Absol.: nam primum ... Non coepisse fuit: coepta expugnare secundum est,: dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet,: Titus Livius hexametri exordio coepit,; cf. : si coepisset a toto corpore,; cf. ; : pro vallo castrorum ita coepit (sc. dicere),: Civilis ita coepit,; ; .—(ε) With an ellipsis for dicere coepi, to begin to speak: ita coepit tyrannus,; : coram data copia fandi, Maximus Ilioneus placido sic pectore coepit,; : tum ita coepit: numquam mihi, etc.,; : ad hunc modum coepit,; ; .—
Pass. in the tempp. perff. and with the inf. pass. (cf. Zumpt, Gram, § 221): jure coepta appellari est Canis,: ante petitam esse pecuniam, quam esset coepta deberi,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 9, 7, 7: quae (res) inter eos agi coeptae, neque perfectae essent,; : bello premi sunt coepti,; .—With inf. act.: mitescere discordiae intestinae coeptae,; cf. Weissenb. ad loc.— Hence, coeptus, a, um, Part., begun, commenced, undertaken. consilium fraude coeptum, : coeptum atque patratum bellum foret,: jussis Carmina coepta tuis,; so, coepti fiducia belli,; : amor,: iter,: arma,; : coeptam deinde omissam actionem repetere,: dies, (cf. infra II.): luce,; 15, 55: nocte,: hieme,. —Hence, subst.: coeptum, i, n., a work begun, a beginning, undertaking (most freq. after the Aug. per. and in the plur.; perh. never in Cic.; also not in Hor.): ut repetam coeptum pertexere dictis,: nec taedia coepti Ulla mei capiam,: coepti paenitentia,; : manus ultima coepto Defuit,: ne audaci coepto deessent; ; cf. : feroci,.—With adv.: bene coepto,: bene coepta,; and: temere coepta,.—Plur.: coeptis meis,: nostris,: immanibus,—Without adj., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Neutr., to begin, take a beginning,commence, originate, arise (most freq. since the Aug. per.; not in Cic.): neve inde navis incohandae exordium coepisset, Enn. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 282 Vahl.): sic odium coepit glandis,: post, ubi silentium coepit... verba facit, etc.,: cum primum deditio coepit,: ubi dies coepit, (cf. supra, I. 2. δ): vere coepturo,: postquam apud Cadmiam pugna coepit,; so, pugna,; ; ; cf. : quando coeperit haec ars,: obsidium coepit per praesidia,: a quo jurgium coepit,; so with ab, ; and with ex, and 68; cf.: quibus, uti mihi, ex virtute nobilitas coepit,.

senses: an undertaking, enterprise, beginning (something started, a work begun)

la:noun:coeptus.html:
coeptus, ūs, m.
coepio
,
a beginning, undertaking (perh. only in the foll. exs.): primos suos quasi coeptus appetendi fuisse, ut, etc., * Madv (cf.: coeptat appetere,): dignas insumite mentes Coeptibus, * .

senses: to begin, commence, make a start
la:verb:coepto.html:
coepto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. and n.
coepio
(mostly poet., and in Tac.; in Cic. in prose only once, apparently for a change with coepit and incipit).
Act., to begin eagerly, to begin, undertake, attempt.
With inf.: diffidere dictis,: oculi coeptant non posse tueri,; ; : contingere portus,: appetere ea, quae, etc., (v. the passage in connection): coercere seditionem,: loqui,; 3, 81; 5, 10: discedere et abire, * ; .—
With acc.: quid coeptas, Thraso?; ; and (acc. to Bentley's correction) : seditionem,; ; : defectionem,: fugam,: pontem,: coeptata libertas,.—
Intr., to begin, commence, make a beginning (only post-Aug. and rare): coeptantem conjurationem disjecit,; : Olympiade septimā coeptante,: nocte coeptante,.
la:verb:coepto.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a. and n.

la:verb:coerceo.gloss: to enclose on all sides, hold together; surround, encompass
senses: to enclose on all sides, hold together; surround, encompass
to curb, restrain, tame, correct, appease
to restrain, keep back, confine, shut up or in, hold in confinement, repress, coerce
to keep within limits, control, limit
la:verb:coerceo.html:
cŏ-ercĕo, cui, cĭtum, 2, v. a.
arceo
,
to enclose something on all sides or wholly, to hold together, to surround, encompass: qui (mundus) omnia complexu suo coërcet et continet,; cf. ; : quā circum Galli lorica coërcet,where the Gallic coat of mail encloses,; cf. of a band holding the hair together,; ; ; : est animus vitaï claustra coërcens,holding together the bands of life,.—
Esp. with the access. idea of hindering free motion by surrounding; to restrain, confine, shut in, hold in confinement, repress (freq. and class.): (amnis) nullis coërcitus ripis,; cf. : (aqua) jubetur ab arbitro coërceri,to be kept in, repressed, (cf., just before, the more usual arcere, v. arceo, II.); , §§ 6 and 8; 47, 11, 10: impetum aquarum,.—Of pruning plants: vitem serpentem multiplici lapsu et erratico, ferro amputans coërcet ars agricolarum,; so of the vine,; ; ; cf. .—Hence, sacrum (lucum), to trim, clip, : quibus (operibus) intra muros coërcetur hostis,: (mortuos) noviens Styx interfusa coërcet,; cf.: Tantalum atque Tantali Genus coërcet (Orcus),: carcere coërcere animalia,: Hypermnestra ... gravibus coërcita vinclis,; cf.: eos morte, exsilio, vinclis, damno coërcent,

: aliquem custodiā,: Galliae Alpibus coërcitae,: miles coërcitus in tot receptis ex potestate hostium urbibus,.—Poet.: Messapus primas acies, postrema coërcent Tyrrhidae juvenes, hold together, i. e. command, lead on, .—

Trop.,
Of discourse, to keep within limits, control, confine, restrain, limit (syn.: contineo, cohibeo): ut (nos) quasi extra ripas diffluentes coërceret,; cf. ; ; ; ; and, the figure taken from bridling or curbing horses (cf.: frenisque coërcuit ora,; and: spumantiaque ora coërcet,): exsultantia,; cf. : Augustus addiderat consilium coercendi intra terminos imperii,.—Of words bound by measure: numeris verba coërcere,.—But most freq.,
Morally, to hold some fault, some passion, etc., or the erring or passionate person in check, to curb, restrain, tame, correct, etc. (syn.: contineo, cohibeo, refreno, reprimo, domo): cupiditates,; : temeritatem,: improbitatem,: rabiem gentis,: faenus,: procacitatem hominis manibus,: suppliciis delicta,: aliquid poenae aut infamiae metu,: omnibus modis socios atque cives,: genus hominum neque beneficio, neque metu coërcitum,: duabus coërcitis gentibus,; ; : verberibus potius quam verbis,; so ; ; v. A. supra: pueros fuste,; : incensum ac flagrantem animum,: licentiam,.—Poet.: carmen, quod non Multa dies et multa litura coërcuit,corrected, finished,.

senses: to unite, come together as a whole
to mass together, ball up, curdle
la:verb:coeo.html:
cŏ-ĕo, īvi or ii (e. g. coierunt, :
coiere,; ; : cŏĭisse,: coisse, ; ; ; pedants preferred conire to coire,; cf. , and Lachm. ad ), ĭtum, īre, v. a. and n.
To go or come together, to meet, assemble, collect together (so mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose); constr. absol., with ad aliquem, ad or in locum, more rar. in loco: matronae ad Veturiam Volumniamque frequentes coëunt,: in porticum,: ad solitum locum,: ad aliquem,: Pharsaliam, * : quo (sc. in sedilia theatri) populus coibat,: in regiam,: in quem (locum) coibatur,: apud aram ejus dei in cujus templo coiretur,: cum rege in insulā,: in foro,: milia crabronum coeunt,; Loers.: coivere amicis animis,; : agmina coibant,; ; ; .—
Poet.: vix memini nobis verba coisse decem,i. e. have passed between us,—
Specif., to go or come together in a hostile manner, to encounter: inter se coiisse viros et cernere ferro,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; .—
Pregn., to form a whole by coming together, to be united into a whole, to unite, combine (the usu. class. signif.); constr. absol., with cum, or dat.
Lit.
Of living beings: neque se conglobandi coëundique in unum datur spatium,; so ; : ut vaga illa multitudo coiret in populos,: qui una coierunt,: reliqui (milites) coëunt inter se,assemble,; so : in formam justi exercitūs,: ut coëat par Jungaturque pari,.—
Of the coition of the sexes (both of men and animals), to copulate, ; cf. : cum alienā uxore,: coisse eam cum viro,: dominum cum ancillā,: cum hospitibus stupro,: privigno,: simul binis,: sic et aves coëunt,; ; ; ; ; cf., of marriage,

infra.—
Transf., of things: membra. ; cf. : ignes coire globum quasi in unum, roll together, as into a ball, etc., ; cf. : sanguenque creari Sanguinis inter se multis coëuntibu' guttis,out of many little drops running together,; cf.: ut coëat lac,to curdle,; : bitumen spissatur et in densitatem coit,thickens,; cf.: gelidus coit formidine sanguis,: semina,; cf. ; ; : tum digiti coëunt,; : ut cornua tota coirent Efficerentque orbem,; cf. : palpebrae dormientis non coëunt,do not close,: labris coëuntibus, et saep.: perfectum quiddam fieri, cum omnia coierunt, necesse est,; ; ; cf. : quae littera cum quāque optime coëat,: ut placidis coëant immitia,.—Of wounds, to close: arteria incisa neque coit neque sanescit,; cf.: potest os coire et vulnus sanescere,; so ; ; ; ; and poet.: an male sarta Gratia nequicquam coit et rescinditur?; .—
Trop., to unite for some object, in feeling, will, conclusions, etc., to join together, assimilate, combine, agree, ally one's self: Caesar cum eo coire per Arrium cogitat,: cum hoc tu coire ausus es, ut ... addiceres, etc.,; : principes, quitum unā coierunt, quantum visum est agri adtribuunt,: heri aliquot adulescentuli coimus in Piraeo (Piraeum ap. ), (consensimus ac pepigimus, Don.): duodecim adulescentuli coierunt ex his, qui exsilio erant multati, etc.,conspired together,; cf.: sed neque cum quoquam de eā re collocuturum neque coiturum: sic, ille consensionis globus hujus unius dissensione disjectus est,: patricii coiere et interregem creavere,: mos est regibus, quotiens in societatem coëant, implicare dextras, etc.,; hence poet.: coëant in foedera dextrae,; : ad nullius non facinoris societatem coibant,; and, like this, with changed construction.—
Esp. of the marriage contract (poet. and in post-Aug. prose); cf.: taedae quoque jure coissent,: conubio,: nuptiis,; : matrimonio,: in matrimonium,; cf.: hac gener atque socer coëant mercede suorum,i. e. in the marriage of Æneas with Lavinia,.—
Act.: coire societatem (cum aliquo or absol.), to enter into an alliance, to make a compact, form a league (with some one; several times in Cic.): utinam, Pompei, cum Caesare societatem aut numquam coisses aut numquam diremisses!; : societatem sceleris,: de municipis fortunis,; : qui societatem in tempus coiit,.—
Pass.: ad eam rem societas coitur,: ad coëundam societatem,; so : si unius rei societas coita sit,; cf. , §§ 2, 9, 10, 15.

la:noun:coercitio.html:
cŏërcĭtĭo (in MSS. also coerctĭo, cŏërtĭo, cŏërcĭo), ōnis, f.
coërceo, II.
,
a restraining, coercing; coercion, restraint, compulsion, chastisement, punishment (not ante-Aug.).
Prop.: coërcitionem inhibere,: sine coërcitione magistratus,on the part of the magistrates,: quo modo judex doceri potest, si desit... interpellantis coërcitio, contentio? * : servorum,: indignamur aliquā admonitione aut coërcitione nos castigatos, id. Ira, 2, 28, 1: vetustissimi mortalium,... sine probro, scelere eoque sine poenā aut coërcitionibus agebant,: an coërceri... cupidines possent, num coërcitio plus damni in rempublicam ferret,.—
The right of coercing or punishing: popinarum,: in histriones,; .

la:noun:coemptio.gloss: A mock sale or purchase, especially one used to free a wife from marriage obligations
senses: A mock sale or purchase, especially one used to free a wife from marriage obligations
la:noun:coemptio.html:
cŏëmptĭo, ōnis, f.
coëmo
, jurid. t. t.
A pretended purchase of an estate which was subjected to a mock sale for the purpose of divesting it of the burden of certain sacrifices attached to it, Moeb.—
Esp., a marriage, consisting in a mutual mock sale of the parties, by which the wife was freed from the tutela legitima and the family sacra, Gai ; sq.; ; ; ; cf. id. ap. ; ; (but acc. to Lachm. ad = 2. comptus, q. v.).
